edition.locus: Vossius 1684 Opera omnia (archive bub_gb_DY2xvRwPetMC), Latin column, chapter I, printed p. 43 (PDF page 67)

source_text: Res quaecunque, aut sensu cognoscuntur, aut intelligentia comprehenduntur: Ex quibus quidem, quae sub sensum cadunt, ipso sensu satis demonstrantur: nam simulatque ille admotus fuerit, subiectae rei imaginem ac speciem nobis repraesentat. Quae vero intelligentia comprehenduntur, non ipsa ex se, sed ex ipsarum actionibus atque effectis percipiuntur. Quapropter cum Anima ex seipsa cognosci nequeat, ex ipsius effectis merito cognosci poterit.
thought_title: How the soul can be known: by what it does
orientation: Gregory sets out how the soul can be known: things of sense are known by the senses, but things of the understanding are known from what they do, so the soul is known from its effects.
pass_a_gloss: Things whatsoever (res quaecunque) either are known (cognoscuntur) by sense (sensu) or are grasped (comprehenduntur) by understanding (intelligentia). Of these, the things that fall under sense are sufficiently demonstrated (demonstrantur) by sense itself; for as soon as it (sense) has been applied (admotus), it represents (repraesentat) to us the image and appearance (imaginem ac speciem) of the thing placed under it (subiectae rei). But the things grasped by understanding are perceived (percipiuntur) not from themselves (ex se) but from their actions and effects (actionibus atque effectis). Therefore, since the soul (anima) cannot be known from itself (ex seipsa), it will deservedly (merito) be able to be known from its effects.

choices.why: The thing set before the sense, not a subordinate thing.

pass_b_english: All things are either known by the senses or grasped by the understanding. Of these, the things that fall under the senses are shown well enough by the senses themselves, for as soon as a sense is brought to bear on a thing, it presents to us the image and form of the object before it. But things grasped by the understanding are perceived not from themselves but from their actions and effects. Since the soul, then, cannot be known from itself, it may rightly be known from its effects.
notes: Edition chapter I ('Quo iudicio comprehendatur Anima').
'intelligentia' rendered 'the understanding' to keep it distinct from 'mens' (mind) in section 8.
'subiectae rei' = the object set before the sense.
No Scripture quoted or alluded to; the work by Tatian's request uses no Scripture testimonies.
